title: Total quotient ring as a product over minimal primes
statement: Let A be a commutative ring [def-weil-affine-spectrum] with finitely many minimal prime ideals q_1, ..., q_t. Suppose every weakly associated prime of A (a prime ideal minimal among the prime ideals containing the annihilator of some element of A) is one of the q_i. Let S be the multiplicative set of non-zero-divisors of A and Q(A)=S^{-1}A [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. Then the canonical map Q(A) \to A_{q_1} \times \cdots \times A_{q_t}, sending a fraction to its images in the localizations at the q_i [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime], is an isomorphism.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 10.25.4, tag 02LX (lemma-total-ring-fractions-no-embedded-points), total quotient ring decomposition; its zerodivisor hypothesis is supplied by Algebra, Lemma 10.66.7, tag 05C3 (lemma-weakly-ass-zero-divisors), with Definition 10.66.1, tag 0547

proof.text: Let $Z$ be the set of zero-divisors of $A$. By [lem-sc-affine-weakass-nonzerodivisors], $Z$ is the union of the weakly associated primes of $A$, and by hypothesis each of these is one of the $\mathfrak q_i$; hence $Z\subseteq\mathfrak q_1\cup\dots\cup\mathfrak q_t$. Conversely, by [lem-pc-minimal-prime-avoids-nonzerodivisor] no non-zero-divisor lies in a minimal prime, so $\mathfrak q_i\subseteq Z$ for every $i$. Hence $Z=\mathfrak q_1\cup\dots\cup\mathfrak q_t$, $S=A\setminus(\mathfrak q_1\cup\dots\cup\mathfrak q_t)$, and in particular $S\cap\mathfrak q_i=\emptyset$ for every $i$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 10.25.4 (tag 02LX), hypothesis that the zerodivisors are the union of the minimal primes, supplied by Lemma 10.66.7 (tag 05C3) with Definition 10.66.1 (tag 0547) and Lemma 10.25.2 (tag 00EU)

proof.text: Because every $s\in S$ lies outside $\mathfrak q_i$ (Step 1), its image is a unit in $A_{\mathfrak q_i}$. The localization universal property therefore gives a canonical ring map $\varphi_i\colon Q(A)=S^{-1}A\to A_{\mathfrak q_i}$, $a/s\mapsto(a/1)(s/1)^{-1}$; the fraction relation makes this well defined, and it is the unique ring map compatible with $A\to A_{\mathfrak q_i}$. Combining the $\varphi_i$ gives the canonical map $\varphi\colon Q(A)\to\prod_i A_{\mathfrak q_i}$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 10.25.4 (tag 02LX), proof first two sentences

proof.text: Apply the prime correspondence for localization [lem-weil-pbc-localization-prime-residue-field-iso] to $A\to Q(A)$: the primes of $Q(A)$ correspond bijectively, via $\mathfrak p\mapsto\mathfrak pQ(A)$, to the primes $\mathfrak p$ of $A$ with $\mathfrak p\cap S=\emptyset$. Such a $\mathfrak p$ is contained in $Z=\mathfrak q_1\cup\dots\cup\mathfrak q_t$, so prime avoidance [lem-weil-pbc-prime-avoidance] gives $\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak q_j$ for some $j$, and minimality of $\mathfrak q_j$ forces $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q_j$. Conversely every $\mathfrak q_i$ is disjoint from $S$ by Step 1. Hence the primes of $Q(A)$ are exactly the pairwise distinct ideals $\mathfrak q_iQ(A)$. Each is maximal: it lies in some maximal ideal, which is prime, hence equals some $\mathfrak q_jQ(A)$; pulling back gives $\mathfrak q_i\subseteq\mathfrak q_j$, so $\mathfrak q_i=\mathfrak q_j$ by minimality of $\mathfrak q_j$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 10.25.4 (tag 02LX), proof third and fourth sentences, using Lemma 10.66.2 (tag 0566) localization-prime correspondence and prime avoidance tag 00DS

proof.text: The intersection of all primes of Q(A) is its nilradical, by [lem-weil-pbc-zero-locus-eq-iff-radical-eq] with the zero ideal. By Step 3 these primes are the finitely many maximal ideals q_iQ(A), so the Jacobson radical is nilpotent. The product-of-localizations theorem [lem-weil-pbc-product-of-localizations-at-maximal] now identifies Q(A) with the product of its localizations at these maximal ideals.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 10.25.4 (tag 02LX), proof fifth sentence, using Lemma 10.24.1 (tag 00JA)

proof.text: For each $i$, part (2) of [lem-weil-pbc-localization-prime-residue-field-iso] applied to $A\to Q(A)$ and $\mathfrak q'=\mathfrak q_iQ(A)$ (with $\lambda^{-1}(\mathfrak q')=\mathfrak q_i$) identifies $A_{\mathfrak q_i}$ with $Q(A)_{\mathfrak q_iQ(A)}$, via $a/s\mapsto(a/1)/(s/1)$, compatibly with the maps from $A$. Under these identifications the $i$-th component of the product isomorphism of Step 4 is a ring map $Q(A)\to A_{\mathfrak q_i}$ compatible with $A\to A_{\mathfrak q_i}$, hence equals $\varphi_i$ by the uniqueness in Step 2. Thus the canonical map $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 10.25.4 (tag 02LX), proof final two sentences
